motion: Does the synthetic evidence justify adopting the proposed city transit plan?

lockedRoutes.description: Defend adoption through evidence of commute benefits, a staged test of generalizability, and an economically bounded capital commitment.
lockedRoutes.successCriteria: Show that expected transit benefits and staged safeguards make adoption more reasonable than delaying or limiting the plan on the present evidence.

motionBridge.description: The evidence and safeguards jointly justify adopting the proposed city transit plan.

centralBridges.description: The pilot provides meaningful evidence that the plan can reduce commute times.
Staged implementation and a checkpoint adequately manage uncertainty about citywide generalization.
Expected operating savings and contractual protection make purchase economically preferable to leasing.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The pilot benefit remains relevant if its service frequency is maintained.
The resale clause materially limits unrecovered capital if expansion is cancelled.

lockedRoutes.description: Oppose unconditional citywide adoption by challenging sample generalizability and the reversibility of capital committed before the proposed checkpoint.
lockedRoutes.successCriteria: Show that the current evidence warrants at most a limited, reversible experiment rather than an unconditional citywide commitment.

motionBridge.description: The current record does not justify unconditional citywide adoption of the transit plan.

centralBridges.description: High-ridership pilot neighborhoods do not adequately support forecasts for lower-density districts.
Major irreversible spending occurs before the staged test resolves the central evidential uncertainty.
A limited and reversible experiment preserves learning while avoiding premature citywide commitment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Leasing vehicles could reduce sunk-cost exposure during the evidential test.
Resale limits and excluded charging equipment leave substantial capital unrecoverable.

lockedSections.title: Pilot benefit and representativeness
lockedSections.rationale: The opening dispute establishes both the plan's principal empirical benefit and the central challenge to extending that evidence citywide.

proMoves.speaker: Alex Pro
proMoves.proposition: A representative three-neighborhood pilot's twelve-percent commute reduction probabilistically supports adoption if service frequency is maintained.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The city should adopt the transit plan because the pilot reduced average commute time by twelve percent across three representative neighborhoods.

conMoves.speaker: Casey Con
conMoves.proposition: Selection of unusually high-ridership neighborhoods prevents the pilot result from adequately justifying citywide generalization.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The three neighborhoods were selected for unusually high existing ridership, so the commute result may not generalize to lower-density districts.

lockedSections.title: Staging and pre-checkpoint commitment
lockedSections.rationale: This exchange tests whether the checkpoint cures the sampling problem or leaves a separate exposure because capital is committed first.

proMoves.speaker: Alex Pro
proMoves.proposition: A staged rollout with a six-month checkpoint tests representativeness before expansion into lower-density districts.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The plan includes a staged rollout and a six-month checkpoint before expansion into lower-density districts.

conMoves.speaker: Casey Con
conMoves.proposition: Because major capital is committed before the checkpoint, leasing would preserve the test while reducing sunk-cost risk.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Leasing vehicles for the first stage would preserve the same evidential test while reducing the sunk-cost risk.

lockedSections.title: Purchase economics and resale limits
lockedSections.rationale: The parties directly compare leasing costs with the purchase contract's protection and then test whether that protection covers the irreversible costs.

proMoves.speaker: Alex Pro
proMoves.proposition: Because leasing costs twenty percent more and purchase includes resale protection, purchase is preferable absent substantially higher cancellation risk.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The lease alternative costs twenty percent more during the first year, and the purchase contract includes a resale clause.

conMoves.speaker: Casey Con
conMoves.proposition: A sixty-percent resale ceiling and exclusion of charging equipment leave much of the irreversible cost unprotected.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The resale clause returns at most sixty percent of purchase price and excludes specialized charging equipment.

lockedSections.title: Net savings and residual forecast uncertainty
lockedSections.rationale: The closing exchange weighs total savings against unrecovered capital and determines whether the same sample problem still limits the final adoption claim.

proMoves.speaker: Alex Pro
proMoves.proposition: Projected two-year operating savings exceed maximum unrecovered capital, subject to the ridership forecast and checkpoint results.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The projected two-year operating savings exceed the maximum unrecovered capital under the cancellation scenario.

conMoves.speaker: Casey Con
conMoves.proposition: Because the ridership forecast derives from the same high-ridership sample, the record warrants only a limited experiment, not unconditional citywide commitment.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The plan is reasonable as a limited experiment; the current record still does not warrant an unconditional citywide commitment.
